Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus is a seventy-one-year-old retired insurance agent, single, who presented to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 39, indicating moderate PTSD symptoms that have persisted for decades. His trauma originates in childhood physical abuse perpetrated by his father, a man who drank heavily and became unpredictably violent. Marcus recalls being struck with a belt, pushed against walls, and threatened with worse if he made a sound or told anyone. The violence was often preceded by the smell of whiskey on his father's breath-a sensory signature that became fused with terror and helplessness. His mother, whom he had depended on for protection, ultimately did nothing to stop it. By adolescence Marcus had learned to make himself small, to anticipate danger in every raised voice, and to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that those closest to him could not be trusted. Once he had settled into the conviction that danger was everywhere and that people could not be trusted, almost anything in his environment began to confirm it-a stranger's glance, the tone of a colleague's voice, the creak of the building settling at night. His belief had become a lens through which ordinary stimuli were now read as threatening.

For decades Marcus functioned adequately. He built a career in insurance, maintained a professional demeanor, and lived alone-a choice that felt safer than the vulnerability of partnership. But in his late sixties, as he moved toward retirement, the symptoms that had always simmered beneath the surface began to intensify. The traumatic memories themselves became intrusive and vivid, appearing without warning as sudden fragments-a flash of his father's face, the sensation of impact, the acrid smell of alcohol-that felt more real and immediate than his ordinary recollections. These fragments would arrive unbidden while he was at his desk or driving home, and they would grip him with the same terror he had felt as a child. When he encountered the smell of alcohol in public-a colleague's breath after lunch, a stranger in the grocery store-the memories became overwhelming, and his body would flood with panic as if the danger were happening in the present moment. Each time the smell of whiskey caught him unaware, it arrived with a thought, quiet and absolute: This is what your life is now-a body that cannot be trusted, a world where danger hides in ordinary moments. The triggers had become proof of something he could no longer argue with: that he was fundamentally unsafe. Each time the smell of whiskey caught him unaware, it arrived with a thought, quiet and absolute: This is what your life is now-a body that cannot be trusted, a world where danger hides in ordinary moments. The triggers had become proof of something he could no longer argue with: that he was fundamentally unsafe.

The intrusive memories and their sensory vividness deepened Marcus's conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him and his body. He had come to believe that his own physiology was a betrayer-his racing heart, his shallow breathing, his hypervigilance were proof that danger was real, even when his rational mind knew he was safe at home. This sense of bodily betrayal fed a growing preoccupation with threat. He began to listen intently for sounds in his apartment-a footstep in the hallway, a door closing, the creak of the building settling-and he interpreted these ordinary noises as potential intrusions. He felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in benign situations, like a cashier handing him change or a neighbor greeting him in the lobby. A stranger's unexpected greeting in the lobby told him, with a logic he couldn't argue with, that people were inherently unpredictable and that nowhere-not even his own building-was truly safe. His vigilance was exhausting, and it was also utterly convincing; his body's alarm responses felt like evidence that danger was everywhere.

The more Marcus's threat system activated, the more his memories intruded. Each moment of panic seemed to pull up new fragments of the trauma, and each memory fragment triggered a fresh wave of threat perception. To manage the unbearable cycle, he developed rituals and mental strategies. He began to perform small mental acts-counting in patterns, repeating phrases-as if these rituals could prevent something terrible from happening again. He kept his mind occupied constantly, filling every gap with work, podcasts, or mental tasks, anything to prevent the memories from surfacing. He avoided television and news, refusing to watch anything that resembled violence or family conflict. These strategies provided temporary relief, but they also reinforced his core belief that he was in danger and that only constant vigilance and these private rituals could keep him safe. The fact that he still needed to perform the counting, to fill every silence with distraction, to maintain the rituals-that he could not simply relax and trust the day-told him something he could not easily argue with: that the danger must be real and that his body's alarm was justified. Each time he caught himself reaching for a ritual, or realized he had filled another hour with podcasts to keep the memories at bay, the thought crystallized without words: If I were truly safe, I wouldn't need to do this. The fact that I still do proves I'm not. Each ritual that seemed to work only deepened his certainty that without it, something catastrophic would occur.

The avoidance and magical thinking, however, deepened his sense that the threat was real and that his body's reactions were justified. His rituals seemed to work in the moment-nothing bad happened-and this apparent success convinced him that the danger was genuine and that his strategies were necessary. Because he never stayed in a situation long enough to discover it was actually safe, because he always escaped through avoidance or ritual before his anxiety could naturally settle, his nervous system never received the evidence it needed to revise its threat assessment. The safety behaviours had sealed off the very possibility of learning that the danger was not as real as his body insisted. He began to avoid social situations more broadly, declining invitations to retirement parties or client gatherings. The thought of talking to strangers, of making small talk, triggered memories of his father's unpredictable mood shifts and the fear of saying something wrong. Interactions that should have been routine-a conversation with a barista, a phone call from an old colleague-became sources of dread. His isolation deepened, and with it, his conviction that people could not be trusted and that safety lay only in solitude and control.

By the time Marcus sought help, he had become almost entirely confined by his symptoms. He had retired early from his career because the office environment had become intolerable-too many strangers, too many unexpected interactions. He spent most of his time at home, performing his rituals, keeping his mind occupied, avoiding anything that might trigger a memory. He was certain that the people responsible for his suffering-his father, his mother-had never faced consequences for what they had done, and this unfairness gnawed at him. What brought him finally to the clinic was a moment of clarity: he realized he was no longer living, only managing to survive. He hoped that treatment might help him reclaim some part of his life, though he was deeply afraid that his body would never stop betraying him, and that the danger he felt so acutely might be permanent.
